intervention.description: 3 units (gender stereotypes, gender-based IPV, socio-emotional skills), 2 sessions/week for 3 months, delivered in classroom

study_design_full: Quasi-experimental (non-randomized experimental vs control group, pre/post)

effect.direction: Mixed - effective on most attitude/stereotype outcomes, not effective on self-esteem or emotional intelligence
worked_for: Male and female gender stereotypes
Gender stereotypes in romantic relationships
Attitudes toward physical violence and physical violence against women
Acceptance of peer aggression (weak, strong, against men, against women)
Affective empathy
did_not_work_for: Self-esteem
Emotional intelligence
Cognitive empathy

key_message: A short classroom curriculum addressing gender stereotypes, IPV, and socio-emotional skills can shift attitudes and reduce acceptance of violence in children as young as 7-9, before they reach the 10-14 age range where dating and partner violence risk rises - though it did not move self-esteem or emotional intelligence, and effects on aggression acceptance were stronger for boys.
limitations: Quasi-experimental design (non-randomized); groups assigned by class scheduling availability
Inconsistent teacher engagement interrupted some sessions
Low family/parent involvement despite intended relevance
Relies on self-report scales, some risk of social desirability bias
No follow-up measurement beyond immediate post-test (no medium/long-term data)
Single school, single country - limited generalizability

intervention_name: Community mobilisation for domestic violence prevention (SNEHA-TARA)

population.age_range: Women 15-49 years (survey population); men, women, and young people participated in groups
population.sex: Mixed (women's, men's, and youth groups; primary outcome measured in women)
population.sample_size_detail: 48 clusters of ~500 households; 3606 women (intervention) and 3592 women (control) in the post-intervention survey

intervention.description: Community mobilisation over 3 years of exposure (delivered 2018-2023, delayed by COVID-19): women's, men's, and youth peer-education groups; volunteer "sanginis" who identify and support survivors; caseworkers providing crisis, legal, and psychosocial support.
intervention.duration: 3 years of exposure (implemented over ~4-5 years including a COVID-19 pause)

study_design_full: Two-arm, pragmatic, theory-driven, cluster-randomised controlled trial; 48 clusters, 1:1 allocation

effect.direction: No significant reduction in measured population prevalence of violence, but a large, significant increase in disclosure and access to support
worked_for: Disclosure of violence to support services (more than doubled: 9.3% control vs 20.9% intervention; adjusted OR 2.75, 95% CI 1.73-4.37)
Over 4000 survivors identified and supported through the programme
80%+ of women who met a caseworker reported reduced violence within 6 months
did_not_work_for: Population-level prevalence of physical or sexual domestic violence (adjusted OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.62-1.16 - not statistically significant)
Population-level prevalence of gender-based household maltreatment (adjusted OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.66-1.33 - not statistically significant)
Community attitudes to violence, gender inequality, and bystander support (trended favourably but not statistically significant)
Population mental health/wellbeing (no measurable difference)

key_message: A well-implemented, high-fidelity community mobilisation programme (women's/men's/youth groups plus trained volunteer responders) can dramatically increase disclosure of domestic violence and connect survivors to support - but did not produce a statistically significant reduction in population-level violence prevalence within the trial period. This is an important caution for practitioners: strong implementation and individual-level impact does not guarantee measurable population-level prevalence change, and attitude/norm change may not be a precondition for people to take protective action.
limitations: COVID-19 paused in-person activities for ~13 months, disrupting a planned midline survey and complicating interpretation
Trial was powered to detect a 6% prevalence difference; observed risk differences were smaller than this
Increased awareness and confidence in intervention communities may have increased disclosure in surveys, narrowing the measured gap between arms
Binary violence measures may not capture changes in severity or frequency of violence
Consent-seeking from cluster gatekeepers may have selected against the highest-violence localities
Two participant suicides occurred in intervention clusters during the trial (investigated, not attributed to the intervention)
quality_appraisal: Not yet appraised (pending JBI review); notably strong methodology - pre-registered, intention-to-treat analysis, TIDieR-reported intervention

intervention_name: COMPASS life skills and safe spaces programme

population.sample_size_detail: 457 intervention, 462 control (wait-list); Sudanese and South Sudanese refugee girls in Ethiopian camps

intervention.description: Weekly life skills sessions (30 total) delivered by trained young female refugee mentors in "safe spaces," plus 8 monthly discussion sessions for caregivers, covering communication, GBV awareness, and sexual/reproductive health.

study_design_full: Two-arm, single-blinded, wait-list, cluster-randomised controlled trial across 62 clusters

effect.direction: No significant effect on the primary violence outcome, but significant positive effects on protective attitudes and social support
worked_for: Attitudes toward appropriate age of marriage (adjusted OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.07-3.28) and age of first child (aOR 2.04, 95% CI 1.25-3.34)
Having same-age friends (aOR 1.71) and a trusted non-family female adult (aOR 2.00)
Reduced child marriage among the subgroup already married/cohabiting at baseline (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.34-0.95)
did_not_work_for: Primary outcome: any past-year sexual violence (adjusted OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.59-1.57 - not significant)
Physical violence, emotional violence, and transactional sex
Feelings of safety at home, school, or in the community

key_message: In a refugee camp setting, a life-skills and safe-spaces programme for adolescent girls did not measurably reduce direct exposure to violence within 12 months, but it did shift protective attitudes (later marriage/childbearing) and expand girls' social support networks - markers considered earlier steps on the causal pathway to violence reduction. This echoes a pattern seen in other studies on this platform: individual and attitudinal change can occur even when population-level violence outcomes don't shift within a trial's timeframe.
limitations: All outcomes self-reported, with risk of disclosure and social desirability bias (partially mitigated via audio computer-assisted self-interview)
Programme roll-out was delayed, so the primary outcome's 12-month reference period overlapped with intervention delivery rather than fully following it
Violence measures were binary (any exposure) rather than measuring frequency or severity
Potential spillover/contamination between intervention and control girls sharing the same camps
A planned longer-term follow-up round was not possible due to funding limitations

intervention_name: Girl Empower (GE / GE+): mentoring, life skills, and cash transfer

population.sample_size_detail: 84 villages, three arms (control/GE/GE+); 1176 analyzed at 24-month follow-up

intervention.description: 32 weekly life-skills sessions with trained female mentors in safe spaces, 8 monthly caregiver discussion groups, and individual girl savings accounts ($2/month). GE+ variant adds a cash incentive to caregivers for girls' attendance (~$1.25/session).
intervention.duration: 9 months of programming (Feb-Nov 2016), assessed at 24-month follow-up

study_design_full: Parallel, three-arm (control, GE, GE+), cluster-randomised controlled trial at the village level

effect.direction: No significant effect on sexual or physical violence despite very high programme fidelity, but significant sustained gains in gender attitudes, life skills, and sexual/reproductive health
worked_for: Gender attitudes (GE: 0.206 SD, p<0.05; GE+: 0.228 SD, p<0.05)
Life skills - HIV knowledge, financial literacy, condom knowledge (GE: 0.224 SD, p<0.05; GE+: 0.289 SD, p<0.01)
Sexual and reproductive health - later marriage, fewer partners, safer sex (GE: 0.244 SD, p<0.01; GE+: 0.372 SD, p<0.01 - roughly 50% stronger with the added cash transfer)
did_not_work_for: Primary outcome: sexual violence index (no significant effect for GE or GE+)
Physical violence
Schooling and psychosocial wellbeing (small, not statistically significant)
Protective factors: social capital and caregivers' gender norms/attitudes were not affected

key_message: Even with very high attendance (girls attended ~28 of 32 sessions) and rigorous trial design, a life-skills, mentoring, and small-cash-transfer programme for girls aged 13-14 did not reduce their exposure to sexual or physical violence over 24 months - despite producing real, sustained gains in gender attitudes, life skills, and sexual/reproductive health. This is the third study on this platform showing the same pattern: individual-level attitude and knowledge change is achievable, but doesn't reliably translate into measured reductions in violence within a study's timeframe. Adding a modest cash incentive for caregivers roughly doubled the effect on sexual/reproductive health outcomes specifically.
limitations: All outcomes self-reported; baseline violence prevalence was extremely high (37% ever experienced sexual violence, 94.8% reported physical violence during the 24-month study period), raising questions about measurement sensitivity as well as true exposure
The trial could not isolate the individual contribution of the cash transfer versus the mentoring programme (no cash-only arm)
Well powered to detect effects on the seven composite indices, but not on individual sub-components
The GE+ cash incentive ended up larger than originally planned due to a study implementation error, complicating clean interpretation of the "plus cash" effect
Set in a specific post-Ebola, post-conflict context (rural Liberia) that may limit generalizability elsewhere

intervention_name: No Means No Worldwide empowerment-based self-defense (COVID-adapted)

population.sex: Girls only (primary outcome population); boys additionally included in one intervention arm
population.sample_size_detail: 15 schools cluster-randomized 1:1:1 (girls-only intervention, girls-and-boys intervention, control); 1540 enrolled, 1250 with primary outcome data; 83% of participants identified as Black

intervention.description: COVID-adapted 'No Means No' empowerment-based self-defense (ESD) program teaching verbal and physical self-defense skills alongside consent/bystander education, delivered in schools; compares girls-only delivery vs. girls-and-boys delivery vs. control
intervention.duration: Not reported in available excerpts (multi-session, school-based program)

study_design_full: Hybrid type 1 effectiveness-implementation cluster-randomized controlled trial across 15 schools

effect.direction: No significant reduction in past-year sexual violence (the primary outcome), but girls' self-defense knowledge significantly improved relative to control
worked_for: Girls' self-reported knowledge of self-defense skills
did_not_work_for: Past-year sexual violence exposure (harassment or rape) - the primary outcome (35% at baseline vs 33% at follow-up, not significantly different from control)
Most secondary/intermediate attitude outcomes other than self-defense knowledge

key_message: A COVID-adapted, school-delivered empowerment self-defense program for girls aged 10-19 in South Africa did not significantly reduce girls' exposure to sexual violence over the trial period, even though it did successfully build girls' self-defense knowledge - echoing a pattern seen elsewhere on this platform where individual-level skill or attitude gains did not translate into measured reductions in violence exposure.
limitations: Programme delivery was adapted for COVID-19 disruption, which may have affected dosage/fidelity relative to the original model
The primary outcome (past-year sexual violence) relies on girls' self-report, with the usual risks of disclosure and recall bias
Conducted in a single city (Gqeberha), limiting generalizability to other South African or regional contexts
quality_appraisal: Not yet appraised (pending JBI review); entry compiled from the published abstract and secondary summaries, not the full text - verify details against the primary source before citing

intervention_name: iCAN Plan 4 Safety: tailored online safety and health intervention

population.age_range: Adult women (exact age range not reported in available excerpts)
population.sex: Women only (recent intimate partner violence in the past 6 months)
population.sample_size_detail: 462 Canadian women recently exposed to IPV, individually randomized to a tailored (iCAN Plan 4 Safety) or static/non-tailored online safety and health tool; assessed at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months

intervention.description: iCAN Plan 4 Safety - an interactive, tailored web-based safety-planning and health tool personalized to each woman's risks and priorities, compared against a static, non-tailored version of the same online tool (both arms received a digital intervention; there was no no-intervention control)

study_design_full: Double-blind, individually randomized controlled trial comparing a tailored vs. static (non-tailored) version of a web-based safety and health tool

effect.direction: Both the tailored and non-tailored digital tools were followed by significant improvement over 12 months on all measured outcomes, but the tailored version was not significantly better than the non-tailored version - this trial compares two active intervention variants, not intervention vs. no intervention
worked_for: Depressive symptoms decreased significantly over 12 months in both arms (p<.001)
PTSD symptoms decreased significantly over 12 months in both arms (p<.001)
All measured secondary outcomes (safety actions, safety-planning self-efficacy, mastery, social support, coercive control, decisional conflict) improved significantly over time in both arms
did_not_work_for: Tailoring the tool to each woman's specific situation did not produce significantly better outcomes than the static, non-tailored version

key_message: A web-based safety and health tool for women experiencing intimate partner violence was followed by significant improvements in depression, PTSD symptoms, and safety-related outcomes over 12 months - but personalizing the tool to each woman's situation did not outperform a simpler, static version. For practitioners weighing a resource-intensive tailored digital intervention against a lower-cost static one, this trial suggests the simpler version may deliver comparable benefit - though the lack of a no-intervention control means neither arm's improvement can be firmly attributed to the tool itself rather than time or repeated assessment.
limitations: No true no-intervention control arm - both study arms received a version of the digital tool, so improvements over time cannot be firmly attributed to the intervention versus natural recovery or assessment effects
Outcomes are self-reported via online survey, with the usual risks of social desirability and attrition bias in longitudinal web-based research
Conducted with Canadian women, a high-income-country population; findings on why tailoring didn't add benefit may not generalize to lower-resource or lower-literacy settings
quality_appraisal: Not yet appraised (pending JBI review); entry compiled from the published abstract and secondary summaries, not the full text - verify details against the primary source before citing

intervention_name: Structural interventions for IPV prevention (systematic review of economic, social, and combined approaches)

population.age_range: Varies by included study (predominantly adult women)
population.sex: Women (synthesis across 16 studies; some interventions also engaged men/couples)
population.sample_size_detail: 20 articles reporting on 16 distinct studies across 9 low- and middle-income countries; 13 randomized controlled trials plus 7 additional quasi-experimental/observational studies

intervention.description: Systematic review applying a 'structural interventions' framework to organize and evaluate economic (e.g., cash transfers, microfinance), social (e.g., group education, empowerment), and combined economic-plus-social interventions for preventing male-to-female intimate partner violence
intervention.duration: Not applicable (review of studies with varying intervention durations)

study_design_full: Systematic review of quantitative impact evaluations, identified via PubMed and Web of Science searches, reference-list review, and expert consultation

effect.direction: 13 of the 20 included articles found a statistically significant effect on at least one primary or secondary outcome (including decreased IPV or controlling behaviors), but effects were inconsistent across intervention types and contexts
worked_for: At least one primary or secondary outcome (often decreased IPV or controlling behaviors) in 13 of 20 reviewed articles
Economic, social, and combined economic-and-social approaches all showed evidence of effectiveness in at least some studies
did_not_work_for: Consistent effects across all included studies - roughly a third showed no significant effect on any measured outcome
Direct comparability across studies, due to substantial heterogeneity in populations, interventions, and contexts

key_message: Across 16 studies in 9 low- and middle-income countries, structural interventions (economic, social, or combined) for intimate partner violence prevention show real but inconsistent promise: about two-thirds of studies found a significant benefit on at least one outcome, but the evidence is too heterogeneous to say which specific approach works best in which context. For practitioners, this is a signal to look at individual studies from a context similar to their own rather than assuming any single structural approach will transfer directly.
limitations: Considerable heterogeneity across included studies in populations, intervention design, and context limits pooled conclusions
Most included studies focused on structural/economic primary prevention rather than interventions specifically targeting adolescents or younger age groups
Review methodology (search terms, inclusion criteria) may have missed relevant non-English-language or unpublished (grey literature) studies
quality_appraisal: Not yet appraised (pending JBI review); entry compiled from the published abstract and secondary summaries, not the full text - verify details against the primary source before citing

intervention_name: Group intervention for male perpetrators of intimate partner violence (pilot/feasibility)

population.age_range: Adult men and their female partners (specific age range not reported in available excerpts)
population.sex: Mixed (male perpetrators plus their current or ex female partners)
population.sample_size_detail: 36 men (22 randomized to the group programme, 14 to usual care) plus 15 current/ex female partners (39% of eligible partners), across one site covering three local-authority areas in England

intervention.description: A 23-week group programme for male perpetrators of intimate partner violence in heterosexual relationships, with an average of three individual one-to-one sessions, delivered by third-sector organisations alongside one-to-one support for female current/ex-partners

study_design_full: Pragmatic, individually randomized pilot and feasibility trial with an embedded qualitative study
outcomes_measured: Feasibility and trial-process outcomes (recruitment, retention, fidelity, acceptability)

effect.direction: This was a feasibility trial, not a powered effectiveness trial - it tested whether recruitment, randomization, retention, and data collection were feasible and acceptable, not whether the programme reduces violence
worked_for: Recruiting and randomizing male perpetrators and their partners into a trial design
Retention and data completeness at 9 months (67% of men, 80% of partners completed follow-up questionnaires)
Participant engagement and self-reported acceptability of both the intervention and the trial design
did_not_work_for: Partner recruitment reached only 39% of eligible partners, below what a fully powered trial would likely need
This trial was not designed or powered to demonstrate whether the programme actually reduces intimate partner violence - that question remains open

key_message: This UK pilot shows it is feasible to recruit, randomize, and retain both male perpetrators and their partners in a trial of a group behaviour-change programme, with reasonably high retention and reported acceptability - but as a feasibility study, it does not yet answer whether the programme reduces intimate partner violence. It's a useful example of the feasibility-stage evidence practitioners need before a full effectiveness trial exists, not effectiveness evidence itself.
limitations: Small sample size (36 men, 15 partners) by design, since this is a feasibility trial not powered to detect effects on violence outcomes
Partner recruitment was below target (39% of eligible partners), which could affect the feasibility of collecting partner-reported safety data in a full trial
Single site covering three local-authority areas in England, so feasibility findings may not generalize to other service contexts or countries
All outcome data, including at 9-month follow-up, were self-reported
quality_appraisal: Not yet appraised (pending JBI review); entry compiled from the published abstract and secondary summaries, not the full text - verify details against the primary source before citing
